title: Self-striping fingerless mitts
subtitle: Fingerless mitts that let a self-striping yarn create the colour pattern.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thumb opening made by working the thumb stitches in waste yarn during the hand, then returning after the hand is complete. The waste yarn is removed to reveal live stitches which are picked up and worked as the thumb.
A method for knitting small circumferences in the round on one long circular needle. The cable is pulled into a loop at the midpoint so each half of the stitches sits on its own needle tip.

content.text: Fingerless mitts in a self-striping DK yarn, worked in 1x1 rib in the round, with an
afterthought thumb
. Sized for hand circumferences of 18, 20, and 22 cm.

Self-striping yarns alternate colour every fixed number of metres so that a small circumference worked in the round produces clean stripe rings without any yarn changes. The pattern is purely structural: 1x1 rib worked from cast-on to bind-off. The stitch lets the yarn do all the visual work. The construction uses
magic loop
on a long circular. Budget about 80 g (175 m / 190 yards) of self-striping DK yarn per pair. Start both mitts at the same point in the colour sequence so they match.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 80 g (about 175 m / 190 yards) of self-striping DK-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, at least 80 cm cable, for magic loop

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: 2: 1 for beginning of round, 1 for thumb position

items.name: Waste yarn
items.qty: About 25 cm of smooth contrasting yarn for the thumb

content.text: Gauge
22 stitches and 30 rounds to 10 cm in 1x1 rib slightly stretched on 3.75 mm needles. Self-striping yarns vary in fibre content; check your gauge against the specific yarn.
Pattern
Before you cast on, circle your size. Every stitch count reads S (M, L) for hand circumferences 18 (20, 22) cm.
Matching your pair
Cut the yarn at the start of a colour segment before casting on each mitt. Begin both mitts at the same colour in the sequence. This produces matching stripes across both hands.
Cast on and cuff
Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 40 (44, 48) stitches. Join to work in the round. Work 1x1 rib for 28 (30, 32) rounds. The cuff measures about 9 (10, 11) cm.
Hand and thumb

Continue in 1x1 rib for 10 (12, 12) rounds. Place the afterthought thumb: work the first 10 (11, 12) stitches with waste yarn, slip back, and work in rib to end. Continue in 1x1 rib for 20 (22, 24) more rounds. Bind off in rib.
Thumb
Remove waste yarn. Pick up 10 (11, 12) stitches above and 10 (11, 12) below. Work 12 (14, 14) rounds of 1x1 rib. Bind off in rib.
Common faults
Stripes do not match between the two mitts: the cast-on position in the colour sequence was different. Cut to the start of the same colour before each cast-on.

Stripes appear as spirals rather than rings: the stitch count is not matching the stripe length of this specific yarn. The stripe length of self-striping yarns is fixed; if the stripes spiral, the circumference is too large or too small for the yarn. Try a size smaller or larger.
Finishing
Weave in all tails on the wrong side.
Care
Hand wash in cool water with wool-safe detergent. Lay flat to dry.
What to try next

The same self-striping yarn on a sock pattern produces matching cuffs and leg sections at fingering gauge. At 3.75 mm the DK version shown here is a good introduction to how yarn colour interacts with circumference.
